findings.mechanism: Empty groups are dropped silently, so when the optimizer has zero parameter groups (e.g., a model with no trainable parameters at all, which is allowed when embedding_learning_rate is set and require_embedding_match is False), the code calls optimizer_cls([]) which raises a ValueError from torch's Optimizer constructor. The PR body claims empty groups are dropped because 'a LoRA run trains no bias and no norm, so both no-decay ones are empty' and expects at least one non-embedding group to exist, but this is not guaranteed: a user can set embedding_learning_rate on a model with no requires_grad parameters (e.g., a frozen backbone) and require_embedding_match=False, yielding an empty param_groups and an empty optimizer_grouped_parameters list; the code then crashes with a torch error rather than a clear message, and on resume the legacy remap's _migrate_legacy_optimizer_state also returns None because legacy_sizes=(0,0) does not match the saved groups, so load_state_dict refuses the checkpoint. The failure is a crash, not silent wrong numbers, but it is a new defect introduced by this change.
findings.trigger: Setting embedding_learning_rate on a model with no trainable parameters (all requires_grad=False) and require_embedding_match=False yields zero param groups; optimizer construction crashes.
findings.consequence: ValueError from torch.optim.Optimizer when optimizer_cls([]) is called; on resume load_state_dict raises because legacy_sizes=(0,0) does not match the saved checkpoint's group count, so the checkpoint is refused.

findings.mechanism: The optimizer.load_state_dict wrapper is installed unconditionally on every optimizer built by _create_unsloth_optimizer, including ones with a single non-embedding group. When the trainer saves a checkpoint for the first time (no resume), torch.save pickles the optimizer, and the wrapper's closure captures the legacy_params list of parameter objects. Because the closure is stored as an instance attribute (optimizer.load_state_dict = load_state_dict) and torch.save pickles the optimizer's __dict__, the closure's captured legacy_params (which are torch Parameter objects) are pickled, which is fine for saving, but the wrapper also persists across processes: on a subsequent save or a checkpoint load in a different process, the legacy_params list is regenerated from the current model, but the saved state's param_groups are the ones saved at save time, and if the model has been modified (e.g., a new layer added) the legacy_sizes tuple is recomputed and may not match the saved groups, so _migrate_legacy_optimizer_state returns None and load_state_dict falls through to the original torch load, which raises because the group count differs. The defect is that the wrapper is not gated on the optimizer actually having a legacy checkpoint to migrate; it is installed even when the optimizer is fresh, and on a checkpoint from a different run with a different parameter set (e.g., a different model size) the mismatch causes a refusal, whereas the PR body says 'Anything that is not exactly the old shape is still refused, so torch raises as it does today' - but the new wrapper makes the refusal happen even when no legacy checkpoint exists, because it recomputes legacy_sizes and legacy_params from the current model on every load, and if those do not match the saved checkpoint (which is the common case for a checkpoint from a different run) it refuses.
findings.trigger: A user saves a checkpoint, then later loads it in a new process with a model whose parameter names or count differ from the saved one (e.g., a different model size), even if no legacy checkpoint was ever involved; the wrapper's recomputed legacy_sizes does not match the saved groups, so _migrate_legacy_optimizer_state returns None and the original torch load raises.
findings.consequence: Checkpoint load is refused with a ValueError from torch.load_state_dict, whereas before this change a fresh optimizer with the same parameter layout would load fine; the new wrapper makes any parameter mismatch a hard failure.

findings.mechanism: The scheduler.__class__ is replaced with a per-class subclass whose load_state_dict closure captures the built optimizer instance. The closure is defined inside the function and stored on the class, not the instance, which the PR body says is deliberate, but the closure captures the optimizer instance (built) which is pickled when the scheduler's state_dict is saved (transformers' _create_scheduler stores the scheduler in the checkpoint's scheduler_state.pkl). On a checkpoint save, torch.save pickles the scheduler's __dict__ minus the optimizer, but the class attribute _unsloth_legacy_resume is a boolean that is pickled as part of the class, not the closure. However, the closure's captured built optimizer is not pickled because it is on the class, so saving works. But on a checkpoint from a different run, the optimizer instance is the current one, and the closure's roles are read from built._unsloth_group_roles, which is set on the optimizer instance, and that attribute is not gated on the optimizer having migrated; the closure's load_state_dict is called on the scheduler, and it reads state_dict['base_lrs'] and remaps them using the current roles, even when the checkpoint is from a fresh run where the scheduler keys are the same length as the current groups; this can pair the wrong learning-rate schedule values onto the wrong groups. The defect is that the remap is unconditional when the optimizer has a legacy checkpoint, but it is also triggered on a fresh run when the scheduler state_dict's base_lrs are the same length as the current groups, which the PR body acknowledges can happen and says 'the latter collapses distinct per-group min_lr floors onto the first', but the code does not actually refuse that; it proceeds to remap, which is a silent wrong-number bug.
findings.trigger: A checkpoint is loaded from a run where the optimizer has a single non-embedding group and the scheduler state's base_lrs are a list of length 2 (the legacy pair), but the current run also has a single non-embedding group and the scheduler's base_lrs are also length 2; the remap pairs the schedule values by role order, which can assign the embedding schedule to the non-embedding group and vice versa, silently changing the learning-rate schedule.
findings.consequence: Scheduler load_state_dict silently remaps base_lrs/_last_lr/min_lrs to the wrong groups, corrupting the learning-rate schedule without raising, which is a silent numerical defect.

findings.mechanism: The function uses id() to map saved param IDs to current parameters, but the saved IDs are stored in the checkpoint as integers (torch's state_dict stores param IDs as the position index in the flattened param_groups, not as Python id() values). The code does saved_ids = [i for g in saved_groups for i in g['params']] and then builds param_of_saved_id = dict(zip(saved_ids, legacy_params)), and new_index_of_param = {id(param): index for ...}, then remapped_state = {new_index_of_param[id(param_of_saved_id[saved_id])]: value for ...}. This assumes saved_id is a Python id() that is stable across processes, but torch's state_dict stores the param IDs as the position in the flattened concatenation of param_groups (i.e., an integer that is the index into the flat list of all parameters), not a Python object id. The code treats saved_id as if it were a Python id and looks it up in legacy_params by position, which is correct because legacy_params is the flat list in the same order, so saved_id maps to the same parameter by position. But the function checks len(set(saved_ids)) != len(saved_ids) and refuses if there are duplicates, which is correct for position indices. However, the main defect is that on a checkpoint from a different run with a different parameter set, the legacy_sizes tuple is recomputed from the current model and the saved groups may be a different size, so the function returns None, but the wrapper then calls original(state_dict) with the original torch load, which raises. The PR body says this is intended ('torch raises as it does today'), but the new wrapper changes the failure to be more aggressive because it recomputes legacy_params from the current model every time, so even a checkpoint that is not legacy (e.g., a fresh run with a different model size) is refused, whereas before the change the torch load would have accepted a checkpoint with the same group count and different parameter set, as long as the group count matched; the new code refuses because it requires exact legacy_sizes, which is a stricter condition than the original torch load, and the wrapper makes the failure occur on any mismatch.
findings.trigger: Loading a checkpoint from a run with a different parameter count or name set, even when no legacy checkpoint is involved, causes _migrate_legacy_optimizer_state to return None because the recomputed legacy_sizes does not match the saved groups; the wrapper then lets the original torch load raise, so the checkpoint is refused.
findings.consequence: Checkpoint load is refused on any parameter mismatch, whereas the original torch.load_state_dict would have accepted a checkpoint with the same group count and different parameters; this is a broken behaviour change.
